misconceptions.description: Writing alt text that describes how an image looks rather than the information or function it conveys in context
misconceptions.trigger: alt text lists colors and shapes but not what the image communicates for the lesson
misconceptions.feedback: Alt text should convey the image's instructional function, not its appearance. Ask what a sighted learner gains, then say that in words.

misconceptions.description: Adding verbose alt text to purely decorative images or, conversely, leaving meaningful images with empty alt
misconceptions.trigger: learner writes long alt for a background flourish or empty alt for a data chart
misconceptions.feedback: Decorative images take empty alt so screen readers skip them; meaningful images need alt that carries their content. Classify first.

misconceptions.description: Relying on color alone to distinguish elements, excluding color-blind learners and those using high-contrast modes
misconceptions.trigger: a chart distinguishes series only by red versus green with no labels or patterns
misconceptions.feedback: Do not encode meaning in color alone. Add labels, patterns, or text so the distinction survives color blindness and grayscale.

misconceptions.description: Cramming a complex chart or diagram's full data into one long alt string instead of providing a longer text description nearby
misconceptions.trigger: learner writes a 200-word alt attribute for a multi-series graph
misconceptions.feedback: Alt text should be brief. For complex visuals, give a short alt plus a longer description or data table the learner can read in full.
